claims.text: Formation and stability of a protective oxide layer govern corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection in Q235 steel during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C.
Q235 microstructure influences protective oxide-layer formation and stability.
Alloying elements in Q235 steel can promote or inhibit oxide growth during high-temperature exposure.
Controlled annealing modifies the microstructure of Q235 steel.
Different annealing treatments can produce differences in grain size and phase distribution in Q235 steel.
Grain size influences oxide-layer formation in Q235 steel.
The distribution of alloying elements influences oxide-layer formation in Q235 steel.
Annealing-induced microstructural changes affect oxygen diffusion during high-temperature exposure.
Annealing-induced microstructural changes affect alloying-element diffusion during high-temperature exposure.
Changes in oxygen and alloying-element diffusion alter the formation, adherence, and stability of the protective oxide layer.
The formation, adherence, and stability of the oxide layer govern Q235 steel's resistance to aggressive high-temperature salt corrosion.
Fine-grained Q235 steel will show less mass loss than coarse-grained Q235 steel under otherwise identical high-temperature salt exposure.
Fine-grained Q235 steel will retain a protective oxide layer better than coarse-grained Q235 steel under otherwise identical high-temperature salt exposure.
An optimized alloying-element distribution will reduce mass loss relative to a suboptimal distribution.
An optimized alloying-element distribution will improve retention of a protective oxide layer relative to a suboptimal distribution.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply to Q235 steel during salt exposure at 700–900 °C.
The proposed mechanism may not apply at other temperatures or in non-salt corrosive environments.
